Software-defined audio (SDA) decouples audio processing and control from amplifier hardware, so that audio features can be designed, developed, managed and updated in software and run on a vehicle’s central system-on-chip (SoC). Much as software-defined networking transformed IT infrastructure, SDA replaces the expensive, single-purpose hardware of traditional car audio, such as DSP-equipped amplifiers, with software on the central computing platform.

The article lists the benefits. Centralized processing reduces the bill of materials, weight, volume and manufacturing cost. Because one software core sits in every vehicle, carmakers can offer different audio configurations across trim levels, or even different audio brands, changing only the amplifier channel count and perhaps adding loudspeakers rather than re-plumbing the whole architecture. Prototyping on SoC development platforms or in the cloud shortens development cycles, and software updates can be deployed quickly.

SDA also opens post-sale revenue. A buyer could start with a standard stereo system and later unlock 3D immersive sound through an over-the-air (OTA) update, or subscribe to premium audio for a road trip. And the in-car soundscape now goes well beyond music: phone calls, voice-assistant messages, navigation prompts, road and powertrain noise control, and different programs for different seats. Running audio as a service on the same SoC that manages other vehicle functions ties sound output more closely to sensors and signals, making SDA a key enabler of innovation and value creation as the industry digitizes.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from “Software-defined audio emerges as key innovation enabler” by Jose Marin of BlackBerry QNX, published in Automotive World. Read the original.
